Karmelo Anthony's bid for new trial over track meet stabbing denied
A Texas judge has denied a request for a new trial for Karmelo Anthony, the teenager convicted of murder for killing a fellow student athlete at an April 2025 track meet.
Anthony, 19, was convicted and sentenced to 35 years in prison in June for the fatal stabbing of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf, in Frisco, north of Dallas. Prosecutors argued that Anthony initiated and quickly escalated the deadly confrontation while Anthony's defense has maintained he acted in self-defense. The closely watched trial drew national attention and was marked by controversy, racial tensions and public demonstrations in support of both families.
After Anthony's conviction, his new legal team filed a motion asking the court to grant him a new trial and remove the judge who presided over his murder trial from future proceedings for multiple reasons, including that prosecutors reneged on an off-the-record agreement during the trial and the judge imposed courtroom restrictions that violated his right to a public trial.
Judge Sid Harle sided with the defense on Aug. 19 and ordered that Collin County Judge John Roach Jr. be removed from the case. But days later, Judge Michael Chitty denied the defense's motion for a new trial, attorneys for the defense and prosecution confirmed to USA TODAY.
Anthony's legal team said in a statement to USA TODAY that they are "disappointed" in Chitty's ruling but "not deterred."
"We will continue to challenge Karmelo's conviction and pursue every legal remedy available to him," the attorneys said in a statement. "We will take these issues to the appellate courts and wherever else the law permits us to go because we believe deeply in Karmelo, in his constitutional rights and in the justice we are seeking on his behalf."
Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis said prosecutors "respect, and expected the court's decision denying the motion for a new trial.
"The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process," Willis said in a statement. "Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing."
Contributing: Mateo Rosiles, USA TODAY Network

sources.news_title: Karmelo Anthony denied motion for retrial after murder conviction
sources.text:
Karmelo Anthony’s defense lawyers lost their motion for a retrial on Saturday following a two-day court hearing in Texas last week.
The development comes two months after the 19-year-old black man was convicted of murder and sentenced to 35 years in prison for fatally stabbing Austin Metcalf, a 17-year-old white athlete, at a Texas high school track meet in April 2025.
Recommended Stories
Judge Michael Chitty rejected the defense’s retrial request after reviewing the evidence and arguments, but he did not elaborate further.
Chitty was appointed to oversee the retrial motion after Anthony’s attorneys on Wednesday successfully removed Judge John Roach, who presided over the trial, from hearing their request for a new trial. They argued Roach should not have done a television interview in which he publicly agreed with the jury’s guilty verdict two days after the end of the trial. That came 28 days before the deadline for the defense to file a motion for a new trial.
Regarding Chitty’s decision over the weekend, the defense is expected to appeal.
“Our commitment to our client has not changed,” lead counsel Russell Wilson said. “We will continue to advocate vigorously on his behalf through every lawful avenue available.”
Meanwhile, state prosecutors hailed the judge’s decision while respecting the appeals process.
“We respect, and expected, the court’s decision denying the motion for a new trial,” Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis said. “The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process. Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”
During the two-day hearing last week, the prosecutors revealed a trove of disturbing texts sent by Anthony on the day of Metcalf’s murder. In one text, the defendant said he wanted to “lick their blood off the blade” after stabbing someone. In another, he wrote, “I’m lowkey on the verge.”
The texts were not disclosed during the trial due to a mutual agreement between both sides to keep questions about Anthony’s character out of the case. Prosecutors pointed to the messages as evidence that Anthony was spiraling in the hours leading up to Metcalf’s death.
Last year, Anthony allegedly stabbed Metcalf with a pocketknife during a confrontation that started over a seating dispute in the stadium bleachers. The defense claimed he was acting in self-defense. The jury rejected that argument. Anthony did not testify during the trial.
Lawyers on both sides told jurors the case had nothing to do with race, but the case drew national attention for that very reason.
JUDGE REMOVED FROM KARMELO ANTHONY CASE AS DEFENSE SEEKS RETRIAL IN TEXAS TRACK-MEET STABBING
Questions about the jury’s impartiality were raised when it was reported that there were no black jurors assigned to the trial. In fact, the trial judge excused three prospective black jurors before the trial.
In a recent appearance on The Breakfast Club radio show, Texas state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the state’s competitive Senate race, pointed to the absence of black jurors as proof that the “system is not working for black Texans.” Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) took issue with Talarico’s conclusion, suggesting the Texas Democrat “sides with the killer” over the victim because of race.

sources.news_title: Judge Rejects Karmelo Anthony's Bid For New Trial In Fatal Texas Track Meet Stabbing - Tampa Free Press
sources.text:
A Texas judge on Saturday denied a motion for a new trial for Karmelo Anthony, upholding the 19-year-old’s murder conviction in the fatal stabbing of a high school athlete.
Anthony received a 35-year prison sentence in June for the death of 17-year-old Austin Metcalf during a 2025 track meet in Frisco, Texas. Following a two-day hearing, retired District Judge Michael Chitty rejected the defense’s request to throw out the verdict.
“Upon reviewing the motion, the record, the evidence and argument, the briefs, and the relevant case law, the Court has determined the motion should be denied,” Chitty said on Saturday.
Chitty stepped in to hear the motion after the original trial judge, District Judge John Roach Jr., was recused. Defense attorneys argued that trial restrictions imposed by Roach violated Anthony’s right to a fair trial.
They also contended that an unwritten “gentlemen’s agreement” between prosecutors and defense counsel broke down, which ultimately prevented Anthony from testifying on his own behalf. That informal arrangement was intended to exclude certain damaging background information and focus solely on the altercation under the tent.
According to eyewitness accounts given to police, the stabbing followed a dispute under a team tent. Metcalf asked Anthony to move because the tent was reserved for Metcalf’s track team. Anthony reached into his bag, told Metcalf, “Touch me and see what happens,” and pulled out a knife when Metcalf tried to physically move him, stabbing Metcalf in the chest before running from the scene.
Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis welcomed Saturday’s ruling. “We respect, and expected, the court’s decision denying the motion for a new trial,” Willis said in a statement. “The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process.”
Had the motion succeeded, Anthony’s conviction would have been vacated, making him eligible for release on a $250,000 pretrial bond pending a new trial.
Anthony’s appellate lawyer, Russell Wilson, said the defense will take the case to the Fifth Court of Appeals in Dallas.
“We continue to maintain that serious constitutional and legal errors denied Karmelo Anthony the fair trial to which he was entitled,” Anthony’s legal team said in a released statement. “The denial of this motion does not make those issues, or others not yet raised, disappear. … We will continue to challenge Anthony’s conviction and pursue every legal remedy available to him … in the justice we are seeking on his behalf.”

sources.text:
Judge denies new trial for Karmelo Anthony in Texas teen’s killing
A Black teenager who was convicted of murder in the fatal stabbing of a white peer at a high school track meet last year will not receive a new trial, a Texas judge ruled on Saturday.
The teenager, Karmelo Anthony, 19, was sentenced in June after an eight-day trial centering on an altercation at a track meet in April 2025, in Frisco, Texas, a Dallas suburb, during which Anthony stabbed Austin Metcalf. Anthony and Metcalf were both 17 at the time.
ADVERTISING
Anthony was sentenced to 35 years in prison. The murder trial and sentencing inflamed racial tensions in Collin County, a predominantly white region of North Texas, and drew protesters outside the courthouse. Some called for justice for Metcalf, while others called for Anthony’s freedom.
After the sentencing, Anthony secured a new legal team to appeal his murder conviction and sentence. After hearing testimony Thursday and Friday, a new judge in the case denied Anthony’s request for a new trial. Anthony’s lawyers had appealed the decision, which will now move to the 5th Court of Appeals in Dallas.
Greg Willis, the Collin County district attorney, said in a statement that he had expected the court’s decision.
“The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process,” Willis said. “Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”
Lawyers for Anthony said in a statement that they would continue to explore legal remedies.
“This denial does not end our work,” Anthony’s legal team said. “We knew when we entered this case that this case might not be won in a single courtroom or with a single motion. We will keep advocating for Karmelo until the justice we seek is obtained.”
In June, Anthony secured a new team of lawyers, who were working pro bono. His new legal team claimed that limited access to the courtroom had violated Anthony’s right to a public trial, that the court had improperly instructed the jury and that prosecutors had prevented Anthony from testifying that he had acted in self-defense. (Anthony has not denied that he stabbed Metcalf.)
His lawyers also made a successful bid to recuse the original judge on the case, John Roach, from additional proceedings after he gave an interview to a local news outlet in which he expressed personal opinions about the jury’s verdict.
Judge Michael Chitty, who took over the case, heard from prosecutors and Anthony’s new legal team this past week. Some of the testimony focused on an informal agreement between prosecutors and Anthony’s original legal team in which they had decided to limit what they would share in court about Anthony’s and Metcalf’s character and past behavior.
Prosecutors had suggested an agreement in which “both sides try the case without character, reputation, or extraneous evidence” for either teenager, Mike Howard, who was one of Anthony’s lawyers, said in an affidavit.
But Anthony’s new lawyers argued that such an agreement had been too limiting during the trial, impeding Anthony’s defense.
For instance, prosecutors felt that the defense had violated the agreement by mentioning that Anthony had been involved in a chess club, according to the testimony of one of Anthony’s original lawyers, Toby Shook.
Howard said in the affidavit that prosecutors had said that “if we called Mr. Anthony to testify, character, reputation, and extraneous evidence pertaining to Mr. Anthony were in play.” Anthony then chose not to testify during the trial.
Testimony on Friday from Bill Wirskye, a prosecutor, shifted away from the agreement and focused on security concerns during the murder trial, such as death threats made against lawyers and others involved in the case.
Wirskye also said that some social media influencers and content creators had been “bad actors” in the case, spreading misinformation to attract views and clicks.

I argued in my spleen vent of the other day, “Pick a Lane and Stick With It,” principles don't magically change depending upon which team you're on.... in this case, which color the kid standing in the legal crosshairs happens to be.

sources.text:
A Texas judge denied a new trial for Karmelo Anthony on Saturday in the stabbing death of a 17-year-old athlete at a high school track meet, a killing that drew national attention and led to harassment of the families.
Anthony, 19, was convicted of murder in June and sentenced to 35 years in prison for the April 2025 killing of Austin Metcalf.
Judge Michael Chitty denied the retrial motion in a half-page order following a two-day hearing this week near Dallas, citing a review of the evidence and arguments. He did not elaborate.
Russell Wilson, Anthony's attorney, said the defense would appeal.
“Our commitment to our client has not changed,” Wilson said. “We will continue to advocate vigorously on his behalf through every lawful avenue available.”
At the center of Anthony’s retrial request was an off-the-record agreement between prosecutors and his trial defense team to keep damaging character evidence about both teenagers out of the proceeding. Both sides agreed to hold back evidence that risked further inflaming a case already boiling with racial tensions and death threats.
The case attracted widespread attention in part because of a flood of social media posts that amplified the killing in racial terms. Anthony is Black; Metcalf was white. Lawyers on both sides, however, told jurors that the case had nothing to do with race.
Worries that prosecutors would renege on the agreement as Anthony prepared to testify, his attorneys say, came after a heated argument between lawyers on both sides and changed their defense strategy at the eleventh hour. Anthony ultimately decided not to testify.
Prosecutor Bill Wirskye defended the trial as fair this week.
“We respect, and expected, the court’s decision denying the motion for a new trial,” Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis said after the denial was announced. “The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process. Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”
Anthony’s attorneys also demanded a retrial because they said trial judge John Roach’s courtroom rules were so strict that they limited the public’s access to the proceedings. And in asking for Roach's recusal, they noted that he gave a posttrial interview with a Dallas TV station in which he expressed agreement with the jury's decision.
“Whatever they say, they got it right,” Roach said.
Roach said his rules were necessary for a fair trial, and prosecutors insisted he did nothing wrong.
Jurors rejected Anthony’s claims that he was defending himself during a confrontation with Metcalf in the bleachers of the track meet.
Anthony and Metcalf were athletes for different high schools in the Dallas suburb of Frisco, where several teams were competing on the rainy spring day when the meet took place.
Anthony sat under the tent that belonged to Metcalf's team, and Metcalf and others repeatedly told him to leave, witnesses testified. That led to an escalating confrontation.
Prosecutors said Anthony provoked Metcalf, and witnesses identified Anthony as the aggressor.
At one point Anthony reached inside a bag and said: “Touch me and see what happens,” according to a police report.
Witnesses said Metcalf pushed Anthony, who pulled out a knife and stabbed him in the chest.

A Collin County jury convicted Anthony of murder in June after roughly three hours of deliberation. The same jury later sentenced him to 35 years in prison for stabbing Metcalf during a high school track meet in Frisco in April 2025.

Hearing on Karmelo Anthony's bid for new trial in track meet stabbing concludes
After two days of testimony, a Texas judge will now weigh whether Karmelo Anthony will get a new trial, following the teen's conviction and sentence to 35 years in prison for fatally stabbing a fellow student at a high school track meet.
Attorneys for both the state and defense took the stand during the two-day hearing on his motion for a new trial, largely revisiting proceedings that happened behind closed doors regarding a "gentleman's agreement" between both sides to keep certain character evidence regarding Anthony and the victim, 17-year-old Austin Metcalf, out of the high-profile trial.
The hearing came after the Collin County judge who presided over the murder trial was removed from further proceedings in the case this week.
Prosecutors called the deadly stabbing "unjustified" and "plain and simple murder," while the defense argued that Anthony acted in self-defense when he stabbed Metcalf at a track meet in Frisco in April 2025.
After hearing four days of testimony, a Collin County jury found Anthony, 19, guilty of murder following three hours of deliberation on June 9. The same jury sentenced him to 35 years in prison after several more hours of deliberation. Anthony did not testify in his own defense in the trial.
Anthony's attorneys claimed in a motion seeking a new trial that the teen was "coerced" into waiving his right to testify, stemming from a purported dispute between defense attorneys and prosecutors about whether his testimony would be covered by the agreement limiting certain character evidence in the trial. Defense attorneys alleged this denied him a "complete defense."
The defense also alleged that Collin County Judge John Roach improperly instructed the jury and that his courtroom restrictions, which limited public access to the proceedings, denied Anthony a fair trial.
In a statement to ABC Dallas affiliate WFAA ahead of this week's hearings, Collin County First Assistant District Attorney Bill Wirskye said Anthony's new, post-trial attorneys "filed a motion containing several inaccurate characterizations of the trial proceedings."
"I and the entire prosecution team conducted this trial ethically and in full compliance with the Court's ruling and any agreements with defense counsel," Wirskye added.
In opening remarks Thursday in the hearing on the motion for a new trial, defense attorney Russell Wilson said Anthony decided not to testify because he believed the prosecution would not adhere to the unrecorded agreement not to question him about his past behavior, beyond what happened during the confrontation at the track meet, WFAA reported.
Wirskye, meanwhile, said he offered the agreement to "stay away from historical character and stick to the facts -- what happened under the tent" in order to "keep the peace" amid what he said was intense public vitriol over the case that led to threats against both sides, WFAA reported. He said the trial defense attorneys agreed to it, and that the "agreement was held."
Wirskye also pushed back on defense claims that Anthony had insufficient time to decide whether to testify and noted that prosecutors wanted him to take the stand, saying, "There's nothing better in my business than a testifying defendant," WFAA reported.
On the first day of the hearing Thursday, the defense called Derrick Jackson, the former Collin County public information officer, to discuss the courtroom protocols, and Mike Howard, one of Anthony's trial attorneys, who detailed some of the damaging character evidence regarding the defendant and victim that wasn't brought up in the trial.
Testimony in the hearing resumed Friday, with another defense attorney from the trial, Toby Shook, on the stand. When asked by Wirskye if there was a "miscommunication of both sides" regarding the agreement, Shook said there was a disagreement, WFAA reported. Shook said he felt the deal was off after the prosecution asked if the defense's mention about Anthony playing chess during opening statements in the trial "opened the door" to character evidence, according to WFAA.
After the defense rested, Wirskye testified about the case and defended the agreement, saying it was beneficial to both sides. He discussed security concerns, citing threats the Anthony and Metcalf families had received amid intense social media interest in the case, and testified that there was evidence that, if made public, could have threatened security, put Anthony at risk and influenced the jury pool, WFAA reported.
"I knew this case was going to be racially charged, divisive, and media would make it about race," he said, per WFAA. Anthony is Black; Metcalf was white. Prosecutors and the defense told jurors during the trial that the altercation had nothing to do with race.
Wirskye detailed more character evidence on Anthony that the jury never saw and maintained that the state held to the agreement. He also testified that he did not say that the defense "opened the door" in those words, WFAA reported.
The hearing concluded Friday evening. Retired Kaufman County District Judge Michael Chitty, the judge who presided over the proceedings, is expected to make a decision on whether to grant the new trial by Monday, WFAA reported.
Chitty was assigned to oversee the case after Judge Sid Harle granted the defense's motion to recuse Roach from any further matters in the Anthony case.
In his order issued Wednesday, Harle wrote that there were grounds for recusal "in that the evidence adduced at the hearing is such that the respondent judge's impartiality might reasonably be questioned."
In the defense motion seeking to recuse the trial judge from the post-trial proceedings, Anthony's attorneys questioned both Roach's impartiality in the case and his courtroom restrictions.
The motion cited what it called "problematic comments" Roach made during an interview following the verdict, in which it said the judge "endorsed the jury's guilty verdict" and defended his courtroom restrictions. It also pointed to a public letter Roach released following the trial, in which he stated that those who worked on the case "contributed to ensuring the process was conducted fairly."
Anthony's attorneys said Wednesday that they are "pleased" with Harle's decision to recuse Roach and "look forward to presenting the merits of Karmelo's motion for a new trial to a fair and independent judge."
Ahead of the trial, Roach imposed a gag order and barred any electronics, including cameras, from the courtroom during the proceedings due to the attention the case had garnered.
"Due to the significant public and media interest in this case, the Court finds that specific procedures are necessary to ensure the Defendant's right to a fair and impartial trial, the orderly administration of justice, the safety and security of all participants, and reasonable public access consistent with constitutional requirements," Roach wrote in a May order.
On Wednesday, Chitty ordered that the trial procedures will remain in effect at this time for future proceedings in the case.

According to a police report, Anthony responded: "touch me and see what happens."

"Yeah, they did, whatever they say, they got it right."
Anthony's lawyers seized on the remark, arguing it showed bias, and successfully pushed for Roach's removal. A replacement judge was assigned to handle the new-trial motion, and that judge ultimately sided with prosecutors, denying the request.
The defense raised three main objections: that the trial court imposed overly strict courtroom rules, that the jury received improper instructions, and that a so-called "gentleman's agreement" between prosecutors and the defense to limit certain evidence presented to the jury had been violated or had otherwise compromised the proceedings. The specifics of each argument were not detailed in the New York Post's reporting, but the judge found none of them sufficient to warrant a second trial.
Among the most striking revelations from the new-trial hearings was the 2023 text message in which Anthony threatened to "shoot the school up." Prosecutors introduced it not as evidence in a retrial but during the hearings themselves, as part of a broader trove of material the jury had never been shown.
The existence of that text raises its own questions. If prosecutors had the message before trial, why was it excluded from the jury's consideration? The gentleman's agreement between the two sides to withhold certain evidence from jurors may explain the omission, but the full scope of what was kept back, and why, remains unclear.
The case has generated harassment and threats directed at both the Anthony and Metcalf families, though the sources and specifics of those threats have not been publicly detailed. The volatile atmosphere around the trial extended beyond the families: one man, Jake Lang, was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill Anthony after a livestream captured a remark about a "headshot."
Meanwhile, the victim's father publicly condemned a former school superintendent for allowing Anthony to attend a graduation ceremony, a decision that struck many as a gratuitous insult to the Metcalf family. That episode drew national attention and deepened the sense that institutions were failing to respect the gravity of what happened.
With the new-trial motion denied, Anthony remains convicted and sentenced to 35 years. His legal team has not publicly outlined their next move. An appeal to a higher court is the standard path, but nothing in the available record confirms whether one has been filed or is planned.
Several questions linger. The replacement judge who denied the motion has not been publicly identified. The precise courtroom rules and jury instructions that the defense challenged have not been spelled out in detail. And the full contents of the gentleman's agreement, what evidence it kept from jurors and on whose initiative, remain murky.
None of that changes the core facts. A 17-year-old was told to leave a tent that wasn't his. He refused, issued a threat, and when the confrontation turned physical, he pulled a knife and took a life. A jury heard the case and convicted him. A second judge reviewed the objections and found no reason to start over.
When the system works the way it's supposed to, when juries weigh evidence, judges follow the law, and convicted killers stay convicted, the least anyone can do is let the result stand.
